idiom_name: struct holding the state plus its pthread_mutex_t, reached only through functions
implementation_notes: C has no encapsulation, so the guardian is a struct that keeps the shared state and a `pthread_mutex_t` (or a C11 `mtx_t`) together, plus a set of functions that are the only code touching the fields - every one of them locks, mutates, and unlocks, and the header never exposes the mutable fields. The classic structure is fully load-bearing here because there is no language feature that replaces it; what must be chosen deliberately is the mutex type, since POSIX leaves behaviour undefined in the cases that matter: a NORMAL mutex deadlocks on re-lock and makes unlocking a foreign mutex undefined behaviour, an ERRORCHECK mutex turns both into errors, a ROBUST mutex hands the lock to the next thread as EOWNERDEAD when the owner died and makes that thread responsible for repairing the state. Where only a single field is shared, an atomic from <stdatomic.h> in the struct replaces the mutex - but as soon as the invariant spans two fields, the guardian is needed.
pitfalls: Returning early without unlocking leaks the mutex forever (pthread mutexes are not recursive by default, so the next call self-deadlocks); unlock on every exit path, or wrap the region in a guard helper.
Nothing in the language stops a caller from reading `a->balance` directly or copying the struct - keeping the state in the .c file behind an opaque pointer is the only enforcement available.
Initialising, copying or destroying the mutex per use is undefined behaviour; initialise it once at construction and destroy it only after every thread that uses the account has been joined.
